in.other_title: ICM elicits superhuman author-gender prediction: 80% vs 60% for human labels
in.rationale: Michael et al. note inductive or tacit knowledge may not admit short justifications and that alternative extraction methods may be needed. Wen et al. report ICM elicits a pretrained model's author-gender prediction at 80% (matching golden labels) while human labels reach only 60%; this is unsupervised label elicitation, not debate, and correctness is checked with golden labels. No cited passage shows author-gender prediction to be knowledge that lacks short justifications, so Wen et al.'s result does not bear on Michael et al.'s question, and Michael et al.'s question does not bear on Wen et al.'s result.

text: The authors note that in their debates debaters justify positions with a few claims grounded in textual evidence and need to reveal only about 3.5% of the story on average in their human debates, but certain kinds of knowledge, such as knowledge of very complex patterns, knowledge induced from many examples, expert intuition, linguistic knowledge or task know-how, may not admit such simple explanations, or debaters may not know how to justify it succinctly. They state that testing debate on questions about such knowledge, or designing alternative extraction methods, may be needed to know whether it can be reliably extracted from AI systems.
title: Can debate extract inductive or tacit knowledge that lacks short, citeable justifications?
